gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the four picks' lithium charge voltages side by side. Victron's Li-ion mode stops at 14.2 V and then holds the battery at 13.5 V with no float, while the Redodo and LiTime 20 A chargers go to 14.6 V and then shut off. Peak charging power is about 213 W for the Victron 12/15 (15 A × 14.2 V) against about 292 W for the 20 A units (20 A × 14.6 V), and Victron gives full rated output only up to 30 °C.
standout_why: Victron's technical-specifications page (cited by ChatGPT) lists the 14.2 V / 13.5 V Li-ion figures, but only for Victron. powergearguide.com also gives Victron's 14.2 V absorption and 13.5 V storage but never mentions 14.4 V or 14.6 V and states no NOCO lithium voltage. clampandcrank.com states no lithium voltages at all. epicvanlife.com gives only a generic 14.2–14.6 V range and lists 14.6 V for LiTime from a listing title. rvpartsgiant.com states no voltage for either brand. None of them puts 14.2 V against 14.6 V, works out charging power in watts, or mentions that Victron's output drops above 30 °C. I couldn't open gearranking.com (both pages) or solargenadvisor.com because of a TLS certificate error, so I didn't compare against them.
decides: Confirms the 20 A, 14.6 V pick (Redodo 20A at $82.99 today) for a shopper who wants a 12 V LiFePO4 battery filled fast and full. It delivers about 37% more power than the Victron 12/15 and charges to 14.6 V, then shuts off. The Victron fits a battery left connected for months, as on a boat: it charges more gently to 14.2 V and then holds at 13.5 V. It is not the 'faster 15 A' choice its amp rating suggests. Separately, our table's Victron row 'Wakes a shut-off BMS: Not stated by the dealer' should change: Victron's own product page says the charger revives a battery 'even from 0 volts'.
